topic: Deterministic statutory calculation as a non-LLM problem
stem: A treasury team asks for a Claude feature that computes statutory late-payment interest from a published formula, an invoice amount and a payment date. Why does this fail use-case qualification as an LLM problem?

options.text: Claude cannot apply a formula supplied in a system prompt without first being fine-tuned on worked examples.
A fixed rule already yields one verifiable answer, so deterministic code is cheaper, exact and trivially auditable.
Financial calculations performed by a language model are prohibited under standard external audit rules.
Interest figures cannot be returned reliably in a structured response field, so every result would need re-keying by hand.

explanation.correct: The defining property here is that a closed-form rule already produces the answer, and correctness is checkable by re-running the rule. Nothing in the task involves ambiguity, natural-language variation or judgement — the three things that justify paying for a model. A twenty-line function is faster, costs nothing per call, never drifts, and an auditor can read it. Qualification should reject this and route it to engineering. The LLM-shaped part of the surrounding workflow, if any, is interpreting the messy inbound contract terms that decide *which* formula applies.

distractors.A: Rules supplied in context are applied readily; fine-tuning is not required to follow a formula. This confuses 'the model can do it' with 'the model should do it' — the objection is economic and auditability-based, not a capability gap.
distractors.C: No such blanket prohibition exists. Auditors care about reproducibility and evidence of control, which is exactly why the deterministic route wins here — but stating it as a categorical ban is wrong and would mis-teach the qualification test.
distractors.D: Structured numeric output is well supported. Even if it were fragile, that would be an implementation concern, not a reason the use case is mis-typed at the qualification stage.

explanation.concept: A task qualifies as an LLM problem when the input varies in ways rules cannot enumerate, or the output requires judgement no formula encodes. If a task has a single rule-derived answer that can be recomputed and checked, an LLM adds cost, latency and non-determinism for no capability gain. Screen for this at triage, before anyone builds a prototype.
explanation.tip: When a stem describes an input, a published formula and one right answer, the answer is almost never 'use the model'. Look instead for the adjacent step where interpretation genuinely happens.

topic: Sponsor's account of a process contradicted by sampled cases
stem: A logistics operator's VP of Operations describes delayed-shipment exception handling as a three-rule process and asks for it to be automated. Before design, the architect samples 60 recent exceptions from the case system: 24 of them were resolved by a dispatcher phoning the carrier and applying a judgement that appears nowhere in the three rules, and those 24 account for roughly two-thirds of total handling minutes. What should discovery do next?

options.text: Build to the three documented rules and log the remaining 24 cases as out-of-scope exceptions for the pilot, without further inquiry.
Report requirements as unstable and hold discovery until Operations publishes a complete written procedure covering the phone-call exceptions.
Sit with the dispatchers who resolved those 24 cases, reconstruct what they decided and on what basis, and treat that as the requirement.
Ask the VP to arbitrate at the next operations review and issue new written policy covering the missing situations before design begins.

explanation.correct: The sample has already falsified the sponsor's model of his own process, and it has done so on the segment carrying two-thirds of the effort. That segment is not a long tail to be deferred — it is where the value is. The only way to recover the decision logic is to go to the people who hold it tacitly and walk backwards from concrete resolved cases, which yields both the requirement and the seed of an eval set. Discovery exists to produce exactly this knowledge.

distractors.A: De-scoping is a legitimate move, but not here: cutting the segment that carries two-thirds of handling minutes leaves an automation that touches almost none of the cost the sponsor is funding. Scope cuts must preserve the value hypothesis, and this one destroys it.
distractors.B: This treats a normal discovery finding as a blocker. Undocumented tacit process is the usual state of operational work; eliciting it is the job, not a precondition for doing the job. Pausing also spends the sponsor's goodwill on something the team can resolve itself.
distractors.D: Asking the VP to write policy top-down produces a description of what he already believes happens — the account the sample just contradicted. New policy may eventually be needed, but authoring it before observing actual practice bakes the same error into the requirement.

explanation.concept: Requirements gathered from a manager describe the intended process; requirements gathered from sampled real cases and the people who worked them describe the actual one. When the two diverge, the sampled cases win, and the divergence itself is the most valuable discovery output because it is where automation effort will actually go.
explanation.tip: A stem that gives you both a stakeholder's description and a sample statistic is asking you to notice the contradiction. Check which side of the contradiction carries the volume or the cost — that is the side the answer serves.

topic: Protecting baseline attributability against a concurrent process change
stem: A health insurer is piloting Claude-assisted triage of prior-authorisation requests and intends to claim a reduction in turnaround time. The same programme is also replacing the clinician intake form and re-routing three work queues, and the current plan lands all three changes on pilot go-live day. Warehouse history is retained indefinitely. What must discovery secure now?

options.text: Adopt the industry benchmark for triage-time reduction published by the workflow vendor in its annual utilisation study as the comparison point.
Defer measurement until the pilot has run thirty days, so the comparison window matches the post-change period in length and case mix.
Reconstruct the baseline from warehouse history after go-live, since the pre-change records are preserved and can be queried at any time.
Measure turnaround, rework rate and cost per case now, and sequence the intake-form and routing changes away from pilot go-live.

explanation.correct: Two things are needed and only one is about data retention. First, a measured pre-period on the current process. Second — and this is what the stem is really testing — the confound must be removed: if the form and the routing change on the same day as the model, no amount of history lets anyone attribute the improvement. Attributability is bought by sequencing, and sequencing has to be negotiated during discovery while the plan is still movable. After go-live it is unrecoverable.

distractors.A: A vendor's benchmark measures someone else's process, staffing and case mix. It cannot serve as the denominator for a claim about this insurer's turnaround, and using it invites a finance challenge the programme will lose.
distractors.B: Waiting until the pilot is running gives a post-period with nothing to compare it to. A baseline is by definition measured before the intervention; matching the windows on length or case mix is irrelevant if one of the two windows does not exist.
distractors.C: Retention is not the problem — confounding is. The intake form changes what is captured and when the clock starts, so the pre-change and post-change definitions of 'turnaround' will not be the same measure, and the routing change moves work between queues. Preserved rows do not make a dirty comparison clean.

explanation.concept: A baseline has two requirements: it must exist before the change, and the change must be isolated enough that the effect can be attributed to it. Discovery is the only phase where you can still influence the second. Where several changes are planned together, negotiate a staggered sequence or accept that no causal claim can be made.
explanation.tip: The clue is the throwaway sentence about history being retained — it is planted to make the retrospective option look safe. Ask what else changes on the same date; simultaneous changes destroy attribution even with perfect data.

topic: Censored historical outcomes block an accuracy acceptance target
stem: A publisher wants Claude to score pitched article ideas for likely audience performance so editors can prioritise commissioning. Six years of history is available: every published article has full traffic data, but pitches that editors rejected were never written and have no outcome recorded. The sponsor wants an accuracy acceptance criterion agreed this week. What is the most important thing to establish in discovery?

options.text: Six years is too short a history; predictive audience models conventionally need a decade of traffic outcomes to stabilise seasonal effects.
Outcome data exists only for approved pitches, so a target measured on that history says nothing about the rejected population the tool re-ranks.
This is a numeric prediction task, so a gradient-boosted regressor over article metadata — section, author, length, season — fits better than a language model.
The use case is feasible as it stands; run a model-graded scoring pass over historical pitches and calibrate the scores to traffic deciles.

explanation.correct: The available labels are censored by the very decision the tool is meant to improve. A model tuned and scored on published articles learns the editors' existing selection function, and an accuracy figure computed on that set is measured on a population the tool will never be applied to in anger. No threshold agreed on that basis is meaningful. The honest discovery output is that acceptance cannot be set until some rejected-population outcomes exist — for example by commissioning a deliberate sample of pitches the current process would have declined.

distractors.A: History length is not the defect; the defect is which rows have outcomes. Twelve years of the same censoring would be exactly as unusable, and this framing sends the team looking for more of the wrong data.
distractors.C: A reasonable model-selection observation, and possibly right later — but it does not touch the fatal problem. A gradient-boosted model trained on the same censored labels inherits the same bias. Choosing a different estimator never repairs a broken evaluation population.
distractors.D: Calibrating to traffic deciles calibrates against published articles only, which is the censored set again. This produces a confident-looking number that will not survive contact with the pitches editors currently reject.

explanation.concept: Before agreeing any accuracy target, ask which population the labelled data represents and whether it is the population the system will run against. Where historical outcomes exist only for cases a human already approved, the sample is censored and the use case needs a prospective data-collection step, not a threshold negotiation.
explanation.tip: Selection bias in the label set is the classic hard-item trap in use-case qualification, and the plausible 'use a different model' distractor is there to draw people who spot only the surface issue. Ask: for which rows does an outcome exist, and why?

topic: Minimum elements of a testable acceptance criterion
stem: A discovery workshop produces the requirement 'the assistant must be accurate'. Which set of elements is the minimum needed to turn that into an acceptance criterion the team can pass or fail?

options.text: A self-reported confidence-score cut-off, a fixed sampling temperature and a retry-on-failure policy.
A sponsor signature on the design document, an agreed go-live date and a documented rollback plan.
A defined metric, a numeric threshold, a frozen evaluation set, and the grader that scores it.
A chosen model tier, a version-controlled prompt template and a p95 latency budget for the call.

explanation.correct: A criterion is testable only when two people running the test independently must reach the same verdict. That needs a metric whose computation is unambiguous, a number to compare it against, a fixed set of cases so the score is not shopped, and a stated grader — exact match, a rubric, a named human panel — because the same metric graded differently gives different answers. Drop any one of these and the acceptance review becomes an argument about interpretation, held under launch pressure.

distractors.A: These are runtime and implementation settings. A model's self-reported confidence is not a measure of correctness, and none of the three tells anyone whether the delivered system met the business requirement.
distractors.B: These are governance and release artefacts. They record who agreed and what happens if it fails, but they contain no statement of what 'accurate' means, so the sign-off has nothing to be a sign-off on.
distractors.D: These are design decisions that fall out of the criteria, not the criteria themselves. A latency budget is a legitimate separate non-functional requirement, but it says nothing about accuracy, which is what this requirement was about.

explanation.concept: Every acceptance criterion for a probabilistic system needs four parts: metric, threshold, evaluation set, grader. The evaluation set must be frozen before the build starts, or the team will unconsciously select cases that pass. Naming the grader is what prevents 'accurate' from being renegotiated at the review.
explanation.tip: If an option lists implementation settings rather than measurement definitions, it is answering a design question, not an acceptance question. Acceptance criteria are always about how you will *measure*, never about how you will build.

topic: Feasibility spike aimed at the riskiest assumption
stem: A water utility wants Claude to read scanned field-inspection reports — pre-printed forms with handwritten annotations, photographed by engineers on tablets — and populate an asset-defect register. The architect has two weeks before a funding decision. Which TWO activities produce the most decision-relevant evidence in that window? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: Build the ingestion pipeline that moves scans from the document store into object storage, ready for batch processing.
Have a person extract the target fields from fifty sampled scans, recording how often a field is illegible or absent.
Assemble a labelled corpus of five thousand reports so a fine-tune can be scheduled if prompting underperforms on tablet photos.
Run Claude over the same fifty sampled scans and score its field-level output against the hand-made human key.
Produce the deployment comparison between the first-party API and a cloud-provider-hosted deployment of the model.

explanation.correct: The riskiest assumption is that the information the register needs is legibly present in the scans at all. A human pass over a real sample establishes the ceiling: if a trained person cannot read a field from the image, no model will, and the finding reframes the project as an image-capture problem rather than an extraction one. Running the model on the same sample against a hand-made key then places actual performance against that ceiling. Together they tell the funding board what is achievable and what the gap is attributable to.

distractors.A: Plumbing that will be needed if the project proceeds, but it resolves no uncertainty. Building it first spends the whole spike window proving something nobody doubts, and the board still has no evidence on whether extraction works.
distractors.C: Premature and expensive. Labelling five thousand reports presumes the task is feasible and that prompting will fall short, neither of which has been tested. Fine-tuning decisions belong after a prompted baseline exists, not before a funding gate.
distractors.E: A deployment-topology question that arises once the use case is approved. It has no bearing on whether the scans contain extractable information, so it cannot change the funding decision.

explanation.concept: A feasibility spike should be designed to falsify the single assumption whose failure kills the project, and it should establish a human upper bound before measuring the model. Comparing model output against a human working from the same inputs separates 'the model is weak' from 'the inputs do not contain the answer' — two findings with completely different remedies.
explanation.tip: Under a short spike window, discard anything that is work-you-will-do-anyway. The only activities that count are the ones whose result could change the go/no-go answer.

topic: Re-scoping around a data-access approval that outruns the timeline
stem: A housing authority is six weeks into a ten-week discovery for a Claude assistant that drafts replies to tenant repair queries. The data protection officer confirms the maintenance case history contains free-text notes with third-party personal data, so access requires a completed impact assessment — realistically eight weeks. A query-volume audit taken during discovery shows 55% of tenant queries are pure status questions answerable from structured repair-status fields, which are already approved for use. The sponsor wants a signed-off design in four weeks. What is the best next step?

options.text: Scope the near-term deliverable to status queries served by the already-approved structured fields, with the assessment as the phase-two gate.
Ask the sponsor to authorise a time-limited exception to the impact-assessment requirement so the design can be signed off on the agreed date.
Continue the design against synthetic case notes generated to resemble the real ones, and validate against production data once the assessment clears.
Suspend the engagement, stand the discovery team down, and re-plan the whole programme once the impact assessment has completed.

explanation.correct: The volume audit is the decisive fact: a majority of queries need none of the blocked data. That converts an eight-week blocker into a scope boundary rather than a schedule crisis. Delivering the structured-field slice keeps the sponsor's date, produces real usage evidence and adoption learning, and leaves the free-text capability as a defined phase two whose gate is the completed assessment. The assessment runs on its own clock in parallel, so no time is lost either way.

distractors.B: An impact assessment triggered by third-party personal data is not a sponsor's to waive; a business sponsor has no authority over a data-protection control, and asking damages the architect's standing with the function whose approval phase two depends on.
distractors.C: Synthetic notes are generated from assumptions about the real notes, which is precisely the thing nobody has been allowed to look at. A design validated on them proves nothing, and the stem shows most of the value does not require the notes at all.
distractors.D: Suspending discards four weeks of usable delivery on data that is already cleared. Pausing is the right call when the blocked data is essential to every use of the system; here the audit shows it is not.

explanation.concept: When a governance control blocks part of a data set, first measure how much of the value depends on the blocked part. A slice that clears existing approvals often carries most of the volume, converting a hard stop into a phased scope with the approval as the phase gate. Never treat an approval requirement as something to be negotiated away.
explanation.tip: Next-step items usually plant one quantitative fact that decides the answer. Here it is the 55%: if a majority of demand is servable from cleared data, the answer is re-scope, not pause and not exception.

topic: Choosing a de-scoping cut that preserves the value hypothesis
stem: A retailer must ship a returns-eligibility assistant seven weeks before peak trading. Discovery has inventoried nine return reasons. Two of them, 'faulty' and 'changed mind', are 78% of volume and are governed by crisp published policy rules. Of the remaining seven, warranty claims require reading individual supplier contracts and a legal sign-off that has not started. The stated value hypothesis is deflecting routine returns contacts from the call centre. Which de-scoping decision is right?

options.text: Ship all nine return reasons and lower the accuracy acceptance threshold so the long-tail reasons can clear the gate before peak.
Ship the seven low-volume reasons first, because those are the ones agents find hardest and where assistance is most valuable per case.
Ship the two high-volume reasons, 'faulty' and 'changed mind', with a deterministic hand-off to a call-centre agent for everything else.
Ship a general assistant that answers from the published returns policy page for all nine reasons and defer per-reason eligibility logic entirely.

explanation.correct: The value hypothesis is contact deflection, and deflection scales with volume. Two reasons covering 78% of volume, both backed by crisp rules, deliver most of the hypothesis at the lowest build and evaluation cost, and the seven-week date is met without touching the legal dependency. The explicit hand-off matters as much as the cut: it makes the boundary visible to customers and agents rather than letting the assistant improvise past its scope.

distractors.A: Moving the acceptance threshold to fit the schedule inverts the purpose of acceptance criteria. It also concentrates the quality risk in the long tail, where warranty answers touch supplier contracts and a wrong answer has contractual consequences.
distractors.B: The 'automate the hardest work' instinct is right in some programmes but not against this hypothesis or this date. Hard, low-volume reasons deflect few contacts, and warranty claims are gated on a legal sign-off that has not even begun.
distractors.D: Quoting policy text is not an eligibility decision, so nothing is deflected: the customer still contacts an agent to find out whether their specific return qualifies. It satisfies the letter of 'covers all nine reasons' while abandoning the outcome the programme is funded for.

explanation.concept: De-scope along the axis that preserves the value hypothesis. Cut by coverage — fewer case types, fully handled — rather than by depth, which leaves every case type half-served and none of them measurably improved. Volume-weighted coverage, not case-type count, is the number to protect.
explanation.tip: When a stem names the value hypothesis explicitly, test every option against it. The trap options here satisfy 'we shipped something for all nine' while deflecting nothing.

topic: Why a lagging business outcome alone is insufficient
stem: A programme defines a single success criterion: 'reduce cost per claim by 12% over the coming fiscal year.' Why is a lagging business outcome insufficient on its own as the success definition?

options.text: Cost per claim is owned by the finance function's reporting line and cannot be adopted as a criterion by a technical programme.
Lagging outcomes cannot be computed from a frozen evaluation set, which disqualifies them as acceptance criteria of any kind.
Percentage targets are inherently unfalsifiable, because the denominator can be redefined at reporting time by restating claim volume.
Confounded by outside factors and arriving too late to steer the build, it must be paired with leading measures the team reads weekly.

explanation.correct: A single annual outcome number gives the team no signal for eleven and a half months, and when it finally arrives it will have absorbed volume mix, pricing, staffing and process changes that have nothing to do with the model. Success definitions need a layered structure: the lagging outcome states why the programme exists, and leading measures — automation rate, escalation rate, per-case handling minutes, first-pass acceptance — move within days and tell the team whether the outcome is on track while there is still time to act.

distractors.A: Ownership is a governance detail, not the flaw. Programmes routinely and correctly commit to a financial outcome; the problem is relying on that measure alone, not who reports it.
distractors.B: Lagging outcomes are legitimate criteria and remain the reason the work is funded. They simply are not steering instruments. Framing them as invalid would push teams to define success purely in technical terms, which is the opposite error.
distractors.C: Denominator gaming is a real risk and the reason the baseline should be frozen and defined in writing — but it is a hazard of any metric, and it is not what makes a lagging-only definition inadequate.

explanation.concept: Pair every lagging business outcome with leading measures that are attributable to the system and observable on a weekly cadence. The lagging measure justifies the investment; the leading measures let you steer. A success definition with only one of the two is either unactionable or unaccountable.
explanation.tip: Distinguish 'insufficient on its own' from 'invalid'. Recall items in this area often offer an over-strong version of the right idea — an option that rejects the lagging metric entirely is usually the distractor.

topic: Low inter-rater agreement in the human labelling baseline
stem: A legal services firm plans to use Claude to classify inbound contracts into fourteen risk categories for triage. Before building, the architect has five senior paralegals independently label the same 200 contracts. They agree unanimously on 61%, a majority agrees on a further 27%, and on the remaining 12% there is no majority at all. What is the most important implication for the acceptance criteria?

options.text: Five raters is too small a panel; expand to fifteen paralegals, recompute the agreement statistic and only then discuss a target.
Score acceptance on an adjudicated gold set with a written tie-break rule, and make the no-majority cases a routing class, not errors.
Set the acceptance target at 88% accuracy, matching the combined unanimous and majority agreement rate of the paralegal panel.
Disagreement at this level shows the fourteen-category taxonomy is not automatable, and the use case should be declined at the triage gate.

explanation.correct: The 12% with no majority have no label, so there is nothing for the model to be right or wrong about on those cases; scoring them at all makes the accuracy figure a measurement of the taxonomy's ambiguity rather than the system's quality. The fix is procedural: adjudicate a gold set with a documented tie-break so the remaining labels are defensible, and define the ambiguous band as a routing outcome — send to a senior reviewer — which is a correct behaviour, not a failure. The 88% band is well-defined and is where a target belongs.

distractors.A: More raters sharpen the estimate of agreement but do not create agreement where the category definitions themselves are ambiguous. Fifteen paralegals will disagree about the same 12% for the same reasons, at greater cost and delay.
distractors.C: Majority-agreement rate and accuracy are different quantities; one measures label stability, the other measures correctness against labels. Treating 88% as a target quietly assumes labels exist for every case, which is the thing the study just disproved.
distractors.D: An overreaction that ignores the 88% where labelling is stable. High-agreement segments are exactly where triage automation pays, and a designed ambiguity route handles the rest. Rejecting the use case discards the majority of the value.

explanation.concept: Measure human agreement before setting a model target. Cases where trained humans cannot converge have no ground truth, and they must be removed from the scored set and turned into an explicit escalation class. Otherwise the accuracy number blends model error with taxonomy defects, and no amount of prompt work will move it.
explanation.tip: When a stem hands you an inter-rater study, the trap is to convert the agreement percentage straight into a target. Ask first whether every case in the set actually has a label.

topic: Mapping a veto-holder outside the sponsor's reporting line
stem: A German manufacturing subsidiary wants Claude to summarise shift-handover notes and flag safety concerns. The design surfaces recurring patterns attributable to individual operators. The plant director is the sponsor and has budget. Which stakeholder must be mapped and engaged during discovery, before the design is committed?

options.text: The works council, since per-operator signals engage statutory co-determination and it can withhold agreement after the build.
The corporate communications team, who own the press release and how the initiative is described to customers.
The vector database vendor's account team, who will size the embedding index and quote the storage tier for six years of handover notes.
The finance business partner, who signs off the cloud and licence budget once the design has been fully costed.

explanation.correct: The specific fact that matters is that outputs are attributable to named operators, which turns a summarisation tool into workforce monitoring. In a German plant that engages statutory co-determination, and the works council's agreement is a genuine gate rather than a courtesy consultation. Because the council can withhold agreement after the system is built, engaging it during discovery is the only cheap moment — its concerns typically reshape what is surfaced and at what granularity, which is a design input, not a launch formality.

distractors.B: Communications matters for adoption and launch messaging, but it holds no approval that can stop a design. Nothing in the scenario turns on external description of the initiative.
distractors.C: A supplier, not a stakeholder with authority over the use case. Index sizing is an implementation detail that follows the design rather than constraining whether it may exist.
distractors.D: Budget approval is real, but the stem places it after costing, so it does not gate discovery and it will not be withheld on the grounds that make this design risky. It is a sequencing dependency, not a veto on the concept.

explanation.concept: Stakeholder mapping must find the parties who can stop the system, not only those who fund or use it. Look outside the sponsor's reporting line for statutory bodies, safety and works representation, data protection, and unions — anyone whose consent is required by law or agreement. Their objections are cheapest to accommodate before the design is fixed.
explanation.tip: When a stem mentions that output is attributable to individuals, and names a jurisdiction, it is signposting an employee-representation or data-protection gate. Sponsors rarely warn you about the stakeholders who can veto them.

topic: Converting a zero-miss demand into a workable requirement pair
stem: In a pharmacovigilance discovery session, the safety officer states that a system extracting adverse-event details from case narratives 'must never miss an event'. The unit receives about 3,000 narratives a month and eleven trained reviewers currently read every one of them; that will not change. How should the architect convert this into requirements?

options.text: Set a precision target instead, since spurious event reports filed to the regulator are what create exposure in this domain.
Accept 100% recall as a hard acceptance gate and hold go-live until an evaluation on a held-out narrative set demonstrates it.
Set a recall target for detection with review retained on every narrative, and measure value in reviewer minutes per case, not cases removed.
Replace extraction with a deterministic keyword search over the narratives against the MedDRA preferred-term list, so behaviour is fully auditable.

explanation.correct: The stem states that every narrative will still be read by a reviewer, so the system is not the last line of defence and does not need to be. That reframes the officer's demand: the safety guarantee is delivered by the retained human review, and the model's job is to make that review faster and more consistent. Splitting it into a recall target the model can actually be held to, plus a value metric measured in reviewer minutes, gives both parties something testable and stops the programme from being judged against an unreachable absolute.

distractors.A: Inverts the risk model. In pharmacovigilance a missed event is the reportable failure; a false positive costs a reviewer a few seconds. Precision matters for usability but cannot be the primary target here.
distractors.B: Perfect recall cannot be demonstrated — an evaluation shows recall on the sampled set, never on the population — so this gate can never be honestly cleared and the programme stalls indefinitely. It also implicitly and wrongly treats the model as the safety control.
distractors.D: Trades the actual capability away for determinism the workflow does not need, since human review already provides the auditable safety net. Term-list matching over free-text clinical narratives will miss paraphrased and negated mentions, making recall worse, not better.

explanation.concept: When a stakeholder demands zero errors, find where the residual risk actually lands. If a human control remains in the path, the model's requirement becomes an assistive target and the guarantee stays with the control. Requirements should then be written as a pair: a quality target for the model, and a separate value measure that reflects what the system is really being bought for.
explanation.tip: Note whether the humans stay in the loop. 'Eleven reviewers read every case and that will not change' is the sentence that decides this item — it tells you the model is not the safety control.

topic: Findings that disqualify a candidate at triage
stem: A telecommunications group's AI council triages roughly forty candidate use cases each quarter. Which THREE findings should disqualify a candidate at the triage gate, rather than being admitted to design as a managed risk? (Choose THREE.)

options.text: There is no way, even in hindsight and with the full case file, to determine whether a given output was correct.
The source data sits in a mainframe with no API, so a nightly batch extract into the group data lake would have to be built.
No named business owner has been identified as accountable for the outcome metric the candidate claims to move.
The current process has never been formally measured, though two years of case-management timestamps exist from which a baseline can be built in discovery.
The output is an exact figure fixed by a regulator's published formula and must be reproducible on demand.

explanation.correct: Each of the three is unfixable by the delivery team inside the project. Without any post-hoc notion of correctness there can be no evaluation, no acceptance criterion and no way to detect regression — the system can never be shown to work. Without an accountable owner there is nobody to define the outcome, adjudicate trade-offs or absorb the change, and such projects reliably strand after pilot. And an exactly-specified regulatory computation is the canonical non-LLM problem: a deterministic implementation is cheaper and satisfies the reproducibility requirement outright.

distractors.B: A cost and schedule item, not a disqualifier. Legacy integration is routine work; a nightly extract is a known pattern with a known price. Carry it into design as a sizing risk and let the value case decide whether it is worth paying.
distractors.D: This is a discovery activity, not a blocker. The measurement does not exist yet, but the data to construct it does, and deriving the baseline from two years of timestamps is one of the first things the team is there to do. A missing baseline only rises to a disqualification where the process cannot be measured even in principle, which is not the case here.

explanation.concept: Triage disqualifiers are conditions the project cannot resolve with money or time: no observable notion of correctness, no accountable owner, or a task whose correct answer is fully determined by a rule. Everything else — integration difficulty, missing measurement, unclear requirements — is work, and work belongs in the plan rather than at the gate.
explanation.tip: Sort each finding into 'buy your way out' or 'cannot buy your way out'. Only the second kind is a disqualifier. Missing measurement and legacy plumbing always look worse than they are because they are visible early.

topic: Splitting fixed-layout extraction from genuinely unstructured input
stem: An insurer receives a particular notification form from brokers. About 90% arrive as machine-generated PDFs from four broker systems whose layouts have been byte-stable for six years; the remaining 10% are scans of handwritten forms from small brokerages. The product owner asks for 'Claude to read all of them'. What should discovery recommend?

options.text: Decline the use case; extraction across mixed print-and-handwriting input quality is not a viable application pattern.
Use the model on the four machine-generated layouts, and template-based OCR with field-position rules on the handwritten scans.
Use the model on all inbound notifications, so there is a single code path to maintain and no template-drift exposure when brokers change systems.
Parse the four known layouts deterministically with a validation check on the fields, sending handwritten scans and validation failures to the model.

explanation.correct: Nine documents in ten are machine-generated with layouts that have not moved in six years — the definition of a parseable input. Deterministic extraction on those is exact, effectively free per document, and reproducible for claims audit. The validation check is what disarms the maintainability objection: when a broker does change a layout, parsing fails loudly and those documents fall through to the model rather than producing silent wrong values. The model is then applied only where variation is real, which is where it earns its cost.

distractors.A: Over-rejection. Mixed input quality is an argument for routing, not for abandoning the use case, and there is a clear, valuable slice — the handwritten tail — that only a model handles well.
distractors.B: Exactly inverted. It spends model calls on the most structured inputs and applies rigid templates to the most variable ones, where handwriting and layout drift will defeat them.
distractors.C: A genuine maintainability argument, and in a truly heterogeneous corpus it would be the right call. Here it pays a per-document cost and accepts non-determinism on 90% of volume that a stable parser handles exactly — and the validation check already provides the drift protection this option is reaching for.

explanation.concept: Split a document pipeline by input variability, not by document name. Structured, layout-stable inputs belong to deterministic parsing with an explicit validation gate; unstructured or degraded inputs, and anything that fails the gate, belong to the model. The gate converts a hidden maintenance liability into a visible, routed exception.
explanation.tip: A stem that quantifies both the share of structured inputs and how long their layout has been stable is telling you the deterministic path is safe. The 'one code path' argument is the sophisticated trap — answer it with the fallback, not by conceding the volume.

topic: Resolving contradictory expert accounts inside a workshop
stem: In a discovery workshop at an energy retailer on billing-dispute handling, two senior agents give contradictory accounts of goodwill credits: one says any agent may authorise up to £50, the other says anything above £20 needs a team-leader code. Both believe they are following current policy. The billing system records the amount and the authorising user id for every credit issued. Forty minutes of the session remain. What is the best next step?

options.text: Adopt the more conservative account — £20 with a team-leader code — as the requirement, since the safer threshold cannot cause an overpayment.
Query recent authorised credits, read the real threshold and approver pattern off the records, and put that rule to the policy owner.
Log both accounts as a requirements conflict and escalate to the billing policy owner for a written ruling before the workshop proceeds.
Facilitate the two agents to consensus in the remaining forty minutes and record the threshold they agree on as the requirement.

explanation.correct: The stem hands you a system of record that already contains the answer, at zero cost and with no opinion in it. Reading the actual distribution of credit amounts against authoriser role settles what practice is, and ratifying that finding with the policy owner settles what the rule should be — evidence first, authority second. This is also the sequence that produces a usable artefact: a distribution of real credits doubles as test data for the eligibility logic later.

distractors.A: Picks a rule on the basis of caution rather than evidence, when the evidence is one query away. If practice is genuinely £50, a £20 threshold routes a large share of routine credits into supervisor queues and the operation will simply work around the system.
distractors.C: Escalating is reasonable, and it is part of the right move, but doing it first asks the policy owner to restate policy — and both agents already believe they are following policy. A ruling issued without the transaction evidence risks re-documenting the same ambiguity that produced the disagreement.
distractors.D: Consensus in a room manufactures a rule that may match neither agent's actual practice nor the written policy. Facilitated agreement is a technique for preferences, not for facts that a database can settle.

explanation.concept: When stakeholders disagree about a factual rule, look for a system of record before you escalate or arbitrate. Transaction data reveals what the organisation actually does; policy owners then ratify or correct it. Escalating first turns a five-minute query into a decision queue and often returns the same ambiguity in writing.
explanation.tip: The planted detail is that the billing system logs amount and authoriser. Whenever a stem mentions that the relevant behaviour is already recorded somewhere, the next step is to go and read it.

topic: Latency envelope that rules out synchronous reasoning depth
stem: A payments processor is scoping automated merchant onboarding. The decision call sits inside a checkout provider's API contract with a 400ms p99 budget for the entire call, and breaching it triggers contractual penalties. The proposal is that Claude fetch the merchant's website, its filings and adverse-media results, reason over them, and return a risk narrative and score inside that call. What is the correct discovery conclusion?

options.text: Feasible if the website, filings and adverse-media results are fetched in parallel and the model's response is streamed to the caller.
Not feasible at all; merchant risk assessment cannot be automated with a language model and must remain a manual underwriter review.
The narrative step cannot fit the budget; compute merchant risk asynchronously before onboarding so the synchronous call reads a stored verdict.
Feasible if the smallest model tier is used, extended thinking is left off, and prompt caching is applied to the system prompt and policy text.

explanation.correct: Three external fetches plus multi-document reasoning cannot be squeezed into a 400ms p99 envelope by tuning, and the penalty clause means the tail is the number that matters, not the median. The structural fix is to move the work off the request path: merchant risk is a property of the merchant, not of the individual call, so it can be computed when the merchant is first seen and refreshed on a schedule or on signal. The synchronous path then does a lookup, which comfortably fits, and the reasoning quality is no longer constrained by latency at all.

distractors.A: Parallel fetching helps, but the floor is still the slowest third-party response, and streaming improves perceived latency for a human reader — there is no human here, the caller is an API that needs a complete verdict before it can act.
distractors.B: Too absolute. Nothing about the assessment itself is infeasible; only its placement inside a hard synchronous budget is. Rejecting the use case discards the value rather than relocating the work.
distractors.D: Reaches for optimisation levers that shave a request but cannot absorb external retrieval plus multi-document reasoning inside this envelope. Choosing the lightest tier to fit a budget also trades away the judgement quality that is the whole point of the risk narrative.

explanation.concept: Feasibility is about placement as much as capability. When a hard latency envelope collides with required reasoning depth, ask whether the computed value depends on the request or only on an entity referenced by it. Entity-scoped results can be precomputed asynchronously, turning an impossible synchronous requirement into a cache read.
explanation.tip: Options offering to tune your way into an order-of-magnitude gap are almost always wrong. Check whether the expensive work depends on anything unique to the request; if not, the answer is to move it off the request path.

topic: Baseline measurements required to test a cost-reduction claim
stem: A grocery chain's supplier-invoice query desk is the target of a Claude assistant, and the business case commits to a 30% reduction in the cost of running the desk. Which TWO measurements must be taken on the current process before the build starts for that specific claim to be testable afterwards? (Choose TWO.)

options.text: The average token count of a supplier email thread, for sizing the context window and the per-call spend.
Fully-loaded cost per resolved query today, including the rate at which resolved queries are re-opened.
The desk's staff engagement score from the annual colleague survey, tracked as a change-management indicator.
Estimated per-query API cost, derived from running a prompt prototype over a handful of sample queries.
The volume distribution of query types, so the share of demand the assistant can address is known.

explanation.correct: A 30% cost reduction is a ratio, and both of its terms have to be pinned down in advance. The numerator needs a fully-loaded cost per resolved query — salary, supervision, systems — and it must count re-opens, because an assistant that closes queries which come straight back reduces first-pass cost while raising total cost. The denominator needs the addressable share: if the assistant can only serve query types making up a quarter of volume, a 30% desk-wide reduction was never arithmetically available and discovery should say so now, not at the post-implementation review.

distractors.A: A sizing input for estimating run cost and context budget. Useful for the design, but it is a property of the future system, not a measurement of today's process, and no cost-reduction claim can be tested against it.
distractors.C: Worth tracking for adoption and change management, and it may well move. It is not a term in a cost equation, so it cannot make or break the testability of a 30% cost claim.
distractors.D: A forward-looking estimate of the new system's cost rather than a measurement of the current process. It belongs in the business case as the cost side of the comparison, but a prototype-derived estimate is not a baseline.

explanation.concept: A baseline must contain every term of the claim being made. For a cost claim that means true unit cost including rework, and the volume share the system can actually touch. Baselining only the part of the process the system will handle produces a locally impressive number that does not appear in the total the sponsor promised.
explanation.tip: For multi-select baseline items, test each option by asking whether the claim could be computed without it. Design inputs and morale measures fail that test even when they are worth collecting for other reasons.

topic: Eliciting with real work items instead of process descriptions
stem: In requirement elicitation, why do experienced architects ask a business team for twenty recent real work items with their outcomes rather than for a description of how the work is done?

options.text: Descriptions give the intended process and omit the exceptions driving most of the effort; real items expose them and seed the eval set.
Real items with outcomes are needed as training pairs for a fine-tune, which a written process description cannot supply.
Written descriptions cannot be held in the requirements repository in a traceable form that model-risk auditors will accept at review.
Working from real items lets the team skip the separate baseline measurement of the current process entirely.

explanation.correct: People describe the version of their job they were trained on, not the version they perform, and the gap is concentrated in exceptions — which is where handling time and error risk live. Real items with outcomes are self-correcting evidence: they surface the exception classes, show their frequency, and reveal the information the person actually used. They then carry straight into the build as labelled cases, so the elicitation effort produces the evaluation set instead of only a document.

distractors.B: Fine-tuning is not implied by this practice and is rarely the first move. The value of real items is diagnostic and evaluative; framing it as training data misses why they are collected during elicitation.
distractors.C: Auditability of requirements documents is not the driver. Written requirements are perfectly acceptable artefacts; the problem is that they are incomplete, not that they are inadmissible.
distractors.D: The opposite is closer to true. Real items make baselining easier by exposing handling time and outcomes, but they do not replace measuring the current process at volume, which is a separate and still necessary activity.

explanation.concept: Elicit with artefacts, not abstractions. Concrete cases, current outputs, exception logs and rejected examples reveal the operating rules that no stakeholder can articulate on request. Collect them early enough that they become the evaluation set, and elicitation stops being a cost and becomes an asset the build consumes.
explanation.tip: Whenever an option ties an elicitation practice to fine-tuning or to audit compliance, be sceptical — the real reason is almost always that descriptions omit exceptions and concrete cases do not.
